title: Authorization
subtitle: Watch one request get checked against roles, attributes, and relationships, then see how tenant isolation stops a bug from leaking data.
learn: How RBAC, ABAC, and ReBAC answer the question 'may this user do this?' differently
Why policy decisions belong in one place while enforcement happens at every door
How least privilege and default deny shrink the damage of mistakes and stolen tokens
Why multi-tenant data needs isolation enforced below the application code

steps.title: Logged in is not allowed
steps.body: Alice works at Acme and has just logged in. She asks for document 42. The system already knows who she is (authentication is a separate lesson). The new question is different: is she allowed to read this particular document? And could a bug show her Globex's documents by mistake?
steps.idea: Authentication answers 'who are you?'; authorization answers 'what may you do, to which thing?'
steps.caption: Alice is identified, but nothing says what she may do yet.

steps.title: The request arrives
steps.body: Alice's browser sends GET /docs/42 with a signed token that names her user ID and her tenant (her company, here acme). The gateway checks that the token is genuine. Then it must decide whether to let the call through. It does not hold the rules itself: it will ask one dedicated policy service, the only place the rules live. One place for rules means every service gets the same answer.
steps.idea: The caller's identity is an input to the decision, never the decision itself.
steps.caption: Gateway receives the request with a verified identity.

steps.title: Roles: what job does she have?
steps.body: The gateway asks the policy service "may alice read docs?", and the policy service looks up her roles. In role-based access control (RBAC), permissions attach to roles and users are given roles. Alice is an editor, and editors may read and edit documents. RBAC is easy to explain and audit. It strains when rules depend on context, because you end up inventing roles like 'editor-of-project-7-in-EU'. Timing here is illustrative: about 1 ms per network hop, and 4 hops make about 4 ms.
steps.idea: RBAC is easy to audit but cannot say 'only her own team's files' without role explosion.
steps.caption: Policy service looks up Alice's roles.

steps.title: Attributes: what is the context?
steps.body: Next the policy service checks attributes: facts about the user, the document, and the situation. In attribute-based access control (ABAC), a rule might say: allow read if user.tenant equals doc.tenant, the document is not 'secret', and the request comes from a managed device. The service fetches the document's attributes (tenant=acme) and sees the tenants match. One rule covers millions of documents, but rules are harder to predict and test than a role list. Facts such as device state arrive with the call from the gateway.
steps.idea: ABAC expresses context-dependent rules compactly, at the price of harder-to-predict outcomes.
steps.caption: Rules compare facts about user, document, and request.

steps.title: Relationships: how is she connected?
steps.body: Relationship-based access control (ReBAC) stores links such as 'doc 42 is in folder Q3', 'folder Q3 is viewable by group eng', and 'Alice is in eng'. A check walks that chain of links from Alice to the document, as the animation shows. It handles nested folders and groups naturally, which is why Google Drive style sharing (popularised by Google's Zanzibar system) works this way. As a rule of thumb, the store should answer these graph queries in under about 10 ms, because every request waits on it.
steps.idea: ReBAC grants access by following chains of relationships, which fits sharing and hierarchies.
steps.caption: Check walks Alice, group eng, folder Q3, doc 42.

steps.title: One brain, many enforcers
steps.body: The policy service is the policy decision point (PDP): it decides allow or deny. The gateway and the Docs service are policy enforcement points (PEPs): they must obey the answer. The gateway asks first, about coarse rules ('may she call the docs API at all?'). Then the Docs service asks again about the specific object, because only it knows which document the call touches. Answers can be cached, for example for 30 seconds: faster, but a revoked permission lingers. If the policy service is unreachable, enforcers must fail closed (deny), so run it redundantly or as a local sidecar.
steps.idea: Decide centrally so rules stay consistent; enforce at every door so none can be skipped.
steps.caption: Gateway asks and is allowed, then the service re-checks the object.

steps.title: Isolating tenants
steps.body: In a multi-tenant system, many customers share the same servers and tables, so every query must be limited to the caller's tenant. Take the tenant ID from the verified token. If a user can pick a tenant, check the pick against the token's memberships. Never trust a tenant ID the client merely claims. Make the database enforce it too, for instance with Postgres row-level security (the database itself hides other tenants' rows): the app connects as a role that cannot bypass the policy and sets the tenant for each request. Here the query returns exactly one row.
steps.idea: Tenant scope comes from the verified identity and is enforced by the data layer, not just by app code.
steps.caption: The query is restricted to tenant acme, so one row comes back.

steps.title: A developer forgets the filter
steps.body: Now suppose a new list endpoint ships without the tenant condition, and the database has no row-level rule behind it. Say the table holds 1,200 documents and Acme owns only one of them. The query returns every row: 1,199 belong to other customers, and even the first page of results would include some. No attacker was needed, just one forgotten filter. Isolation must not depend on every developer remembering a WHERE clause.
steps.idea: If isolation lives only in application code, one missed filter becomes a cross-customer data breach.
steps.caption: Unscoped query returns other tenants' rows.

steps.title: Least privilege and default deny
steps.body: Give each user, token, and service only what its job needs (least privilege), and make 'no matching rule' mean deny. Alice's token carries a narrow scope (a permission label inside the token) such as docs:read, so a leaked token cannot delete anything. The Docs service's database login should not be able to drop tables either. Now Alice asks for a Globex document. The Docs service asks the policy service, no rule allows it, the answer is deny, and she gets a 403 Forbidden (many multi-tenant APIs return 404 instead, so outsiders cannot confirm a document exists).
steps.idea: Default deny plus narrow grants turns mistakes and stolen credentials into small incidents.
steps.caption: Object-level check finds no matching rule, so the request is refused.

steps.title: Who may do what
steps.body: Authorization checks a verified identity against rules. RBAC uses roles, ABAC uses attributes, ReBAC uses relationships, and real systems often mix them. Keep decisions in one policy service, enforce at every service boundary, default to deny, grant the minimum, and enforce tenant scope in the database as well as in code.
steps.idea: Centralize the decision, enforce everywhere, deny by default, and isolate tenants below the app.
steps.caption: Every layer can say no.

quiz.q: A company's rule is 'managers may approve expenses only for people in their own reporting chain.' Which model fits most naturally?
options: RBAC with a single 'manager' role
ReBAC, following manager-of links in the org graph
Authentication with MFA
Encrypting the expense table
quiz.why: The permission depends on how two people are connected. A plain 'manager' role would let every manager approve for everyone; relationships express the chain directly.

quiz.q: Your RBAC system now has 400 roles such as 'viewer-project-12-eu'. What is the best diagnosis?
options: Roles are too coarse and rules depend on context, so attributes or relationships fit better
You need longer passwords
The policy service is too fast
Users should share one admin role
quiz.why: Role explosion signals that the real rule involves resource or context facts. ABAC or ReBAC encode those directly instead of minting a role per combination.

quiz.q: Why does the Docs service re-check permission even though the gateway already allowed the request?
options: The gateway's allow decision only counts if the service re-signs it with a new token
Tokens cannot be verified twice
Re-checking is required by the TLS handshake
Only the service knows which specific object the call touches, and a bypassed gateway must not mean open access
quiz.why: Coarse checks at the edge cannot cover object-level rules, and defense in depth means an internal caller or a gateway misconfiguration does not skip authorization.

quiz.q: An endpoint reads tenant_id from a JSON field in the request body to scope its query. What is the flaw?
options: JSON is slow to parse
The database cannot filter by tenant
A caller can set the field to another tenant's ID; tenant must come from the verified token
It breaks least privilege only for admins
quiz.why: Anything the client sends is attacker-controlled. Tenant scope must derive from verified identity, and ideally be enforced again by row-level security.

quiz.q: After Alice is removed from group eng, she can still read files for about 30 seconds. What is the most likely cause?
options: A cached policy decision has not yet expired
RBAC forbids revocation
Row-level security is disabled
Her password is still valid
quiz.why: Caching decisions speeds checks but delays revocation by up to the cache lifetime. Short TTLs or explicit invalidation shrink that window.

cheatsheet.def: Authentication proves who you are. Authorization decides what that identity may do to a specific resource.
Permissions attach to roles, users get roles. Simple and auditable, but role counts explode when context matters.
Rules over attributes of user, resource, and environment. Flexible and compact, but harder to test and explain.
Access follows relationship paths (user, group, folder, doc). Natural for sharing and hierarchies.
Policy decision point computes allow or deny; policy enforcement points (gateway, services) obey it.
Grant the minimum access needed, with narrow token scopes and default deny when no rule matches.
Take tenant ID from the verified identity and enforce it in the data layer (row-level security, per-tenant schemas or databases).
Caching allow/deny for seconds cuts latency but delays revocation; choose the TTL by how bad stale access is.
